title: Chinese Remainder Theorem (Non-Coprime Moduli)
description: Generalizes the Chinese Remainder Theorem to arbitrary moduli: the system x = a (mod m), x = b (mod n) is solvable iff gcd(m,n) | (a-b), with solutions unique modulo lcm(m,n).

meta.author: Euler (generalization, formalized in Lean 4)
originalContributions: Constructive sufficiency proof via Bezout on reduced moduli
Classical CRT recovered as special case

overview.historicalContext:
The classical Chinese Remainder Theorem requires coprime moduli: gcd(m,n) = 1. But what happens when the moduli share common factors? Euler developed the generalization in the 18th century, showing that solvability depends on a divisibility condition involving the gcd.

This generalization is essential in algebraic number theory, coding theory, and computational algebra, where coprimality cannot always be guaranteed.
overview.problemStatement:
**Generalized CRT**: Given integers a, b and positive moduli m, n (not necessarily coprime):

The system x = a (mod m), x = b (mod n) has a solution if and only if gcd(m,n) | (a - b).

When a solution exists, it is unique modulo lcm(m,n).

**Key Insight**: The classical CRT is the special case where gcd(m,n) = 1, so the divisibility condition is automatically satisfied and lcm(m,n) = m*n.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Necessity**: If x is a solution, then m | (x-a) and n | (x-b). Since gcd(m,n) divides both m and n, it divides both (x-a) and (x-b), hence their difference (a-b).

**Sufficiency**: Write g = gcd(m,n), m = g*m', n = g*n' where gcd(m',n') = 1. By Bezout, m'*s + n'*t = 1. If a - b = g*k, then x = a + m*(-k*s) satisfies both congruences. The algebraic verification uses the Bezout relation to show n divides (x-b).

**Uniqueness**: Two solutions satisfy x1 = x2 (mod m) and x1 = x2 (mod n), so lcm(m,n) | (x1-x2).
keyInsights: The solvability criterion $\gcd(m,n) \mid (a-b)$ is both necessary and sufficient for the system $x \equiv a \pmod{m},\; x \equiv b \pmod{n}$
Uniqueness is modulo $\text{lcm}(m,n) = mn/\gcd(m,n)$, strictly tighter than $mn$ when $\gcd(m,n) > 1$
The construction reduces to the coprime case: set $m' = m/g$, $n' = n/g$ with $\gcd(m',n') = 1$, then apply Bézout
The complete iff characterization $\exists x \iff \gcd(m,n) \mid (a-b)$ gives a decidable criterion for solvability

sections.title: LCM-Based Congruence Combining
sections.summary: If x = y (mod m) and x = y (mod n), then x = y (mod lcm(m,n)). Full iff characterization.

sections.title: Solvability Condition
sections.summary: The system is solvable iff gcd(m,n) | (a-b). Necessity by divisibility chain, sufficiency by Bezout construction.
sections.mathContext: $\exists x \iff \gcd(m,n) \mid (a-b)$; sufficiency via $x = a + m(-ks)$ with Bézout on $m/g$, $n/g$

sections.title: Uniqueness Modulo LCM
sections.summary: Two solutions agree modulo lcm(m,n), using the LCM combining lemma.

sections.title: Classical CRT as Special Case
sections.summary: When gcd(m,n) = 1, solvability is automatic and lcm = m*n, recovering the classical theorem.

sections.title: Extension to Three Moduli
sections.summary: Pairwise gcd conditions are necessary, with uniqueness via iterated LCM.
sections.mathContext: Pairwise condition: $\gcd(m_i, m_j) \mid (a_i - a_j)$ for all $i \neq j$; uniqueness mod $\text{lcm}(m_1, m_2, m_3)$

sections.title: Concrete Examples
sections.summary: Verified examples including solvable, unsolvable, and coprime cases.
sections.mathContext: Key example: $x \equiv 1 \pmod{6},\; x \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$ is unsolvable since $\gcd(6,4) = 2 \nmid -1$

conclusion.summary:
This formalization provides the complete generalization of the Chinese Remainder Theorem to non-coprime moduli. Every theorem is fully proved (0 sorries) using constructive methods based on Bezout's identity.

The key results are: (1) the gcd divisibility characterization of solvability, (2) uniqueness modulo lcm, and (3) recovery of the classical CRT as a special case.
conclusion.implications:
**Algebraic Number Theory**: Non-coprime CRT arises naturally when working with ideals in rings where unique factorization may fail.

**Coding Theory**: Error-correcting codes based on CRT often need the non-coprime version for redundant residue number systems.

**Scheduling Problems**: Finding when multiple cycles with shared periods align requires the non-coprime CRT to determine if alignment is possible.
openQuestions: Can the construction be made more computationally efficient for large moduli?
How does the non-coprime CRT extend to polynomial rings and general PIDs?
What are the implications for simultaneous Diophantine approximation?
